title: Where to Stay in Tokyo: Best Neighborhoods for First-Timers
excerpt: Shinjuku, Asakusa, or Shibuya? Here's how Tokyo's best base neighborhoods compare for first-time American visitors, and who each one suits.
content:
Tokyo is enormous, so where you base yourself shapes your whole trip — how much time you spend on trains, what's walkable at night, and the vibe you wake up to. The good news: the city's train network is so good that any central neighborhood works. For a first visit, three areas stand out, with a fourth worth considering if you want something more refined.

How to think about location

The single most useful thing to know is the JR Yamanote line — a loop that circles central Tokyo and stops at most of the neighborhoods you'll want. Staying on or near the Yamanote loop, or on a Tokyo Metro subway line, means you can reach almost anything quickly. With a Suica or Pasmo IC card in hand, getting around is effortless. So "best neighborhood" is less about being central and more about which atmosphere fits you.

Shinjuku — best all-rounder

If you want one base that does everything, Shinjuku is the safe pick. It's a major transit hub, so trains radiate everywhere, and it packs in dining, shopping, nightlife, and green space (Shinjuku Gyoen, one of the city's loveliest parks) within walking distance. It's busy and bright — the neon-and-crowds Tokyo people picture — with the atmospheric little lantern-lit alleys of Omoide Yokocho for evening food. Great for first-timers who want energy and convenience. The trade-off is that it's dense and can feel overwhelming if you prefer quiet.

Asakusa — best for traditional atmosphere

Asakusa is the old-Tokyo counterpoint. It's home to Senso-ji, the city's most famous temple, and the surrounding streets keep a more traditional, low-rise feel with craft shops and street food. It's calmer and often better value than the western hubs, and you're near the Sumida River and Tokyo Skytree. The trade-off: it sits on the eastern side, so reaching the Shibuya/Shinjuku side takes a bit longer — though still an easy train ride. Ideal if you want charm and a sense of history over glitz.

Shibuya — best for energy and shopping

Shibuya is youthful, fashionable, and endlessly walkable, anchored by the famous Shibuya Crossing and surrounded by shopping, cafes, and nightlife. It connects smoothly to Harajuku and the rest of the Yamanote loop. It's a fantastic base if you're drawn to street culture, shopping, and being in the thick of things. Like Shinjuku, it's busy — that's the appeal and the catch.

Ginza — best for upscale calm

If you'd rather a more polished, grown-up base, Ginza is Tokyo's elegant shopping and dining district. It's central, refined, and quieter at night than the western hubs, with high-end stores and restaurants. It tends to cost more, but it's a great fit for travelers who want comfort and sophistication over buzz.

Which should you choose?

For most first-time American visitors, Shinjuku is the easiest all-rounder, Asakusa wins for traditional charm and value, and Shibuya is best if you want to be at the center of the energy. Ginza is the upscale alternative. Any of them puts the whole city within easy reach.

Hotels in these areas book up fast in cherry blossom and fall foliage season, so it's worth checking availability and prices early for your dates. Once your base is set, the fun part is planning what to actually do.

title: Best Things to Do in Tokyo
excerpt: From Senso-ji temple to Shibuya Crossing to teamLab's digital art, here are the Tokyo experiences first-time American visitors shouldn't miss.
content:
Tokyo rewards almost any interest — ancient temples, neon nightlife, world-class food, and some of the most inventive art and tech experiences on earth. For a first visit, here are the standouts worth building your days around.

Senso-ji and Asakusa

Start with Senso-ji, Tokyo's oldest and most famous temple, in the Asakusa district. You approach through the Nakamise shopping street, lined with stalls selling snacks and souvenirs, before reaching the grand temple gate and hall. Go early in the morning to beat the crowds and catch the calm. It's the best single place to feel old Tokyo.

Shibuya Crossing

The Shibuya Crossing is the iconic Tokyo scramble — hundreds of people surging across in every direction when the lights change. Walk it once for the experience, then watch the choreography from above at one of the surrounding cafes or viewpoints. The whole Shibuya area around it is prime for shopping and people-watching.

teamLab digital art

One of Tokyo's most extraordinary experiences is teamLab, an immersive digital art museum where rooms of light, color, and projection respond to your movement. It's unlike anything else and a favorite of nearly every first-timer. Tickets are timed and sell out, so book ahead for your preferred slot.

Meiji Shrine

For a complete change of pace, Meiji Shrine sits in a tranquil forest right beside busy Harajuku. The wooded approach and grand torii gates make it one of the most peaceful spots in the city — a reminder of how Tokyo balances the frenetic and the serene. Pair it with a wander through Harajuku's youth-fashion streets next door.

Tokyo Skytree

For the view, Tokyo Skytree is one of the tallest towers in the world, with observation decks that lay the sprawling city out beneath you — and on clear days, Mt Fuji in the distance. Go near sunset to catch both daytime and the city lighting up.

Eat your way through the city

Tokyo is one of the world's great food cities. Wander the Tsukiji Outer Market for fresh seafood and street snacks, duck into an izakaya (Japanese pub) for small plates and drinks, and slurp a bowl at a ramen shop — chains like Ichiran make solo ramen easy and fun. Remember there's no tipping, and it's polite not to eat while walking.

More to explore

If you have extra days, Akihabara is the electronics-and-anime district, Ginza offers upscale shopping, Shinjuku's Omoide Yokocho serves atmospheric alley dining, and the Imperial Palace grounds give you a green central stroll. You won't run out of things to do.

Booking experiences

Some of the best Tokyo experiences — guided food tours, teamLab tickets, day excursions — are worth reserving in advance, especially in peak seasons. Booking ahead locks in your spot and saves you time on the ground. And when you're ready to see beyond the city, Tokyo makes a great launch pad for day trips.

title: Best Day Trips from Tokyo (Hakone, Nikko & Kamakura)
excerpt: Tokyo's rail network puts mountains, temples, and a giant Buddha within easy reach. Here are the three best day trips for first-time visitors.
content:
One of the joys of basing yourself in Tokyo is how easily you can escape it. The rail network puts hot-spring mountains, UNESCO shrines, and a giant bronze Buddha all within a day's reach. Here are the three classic day trips, each offering something the city can't.

Hakone — hot springs and Mt Fuji views

Hakone is the go-to mountain escape, famous for its onsen (hot springs) and, on clear days, postcard views of Mt Fuji. A typical loop combines a scenic mountain railway, a ropeway over volcanic valleys, and a pirate-themed sightseeing boat across Lake Ashi — touristy but genuinely fun. Soaking in an onsen with Fuji in the distance is a quintessential Japan moment. It's the best pick if you want nature, relaxation, and that Fuji view in one trip.

Nikko — UNESCO shrines in the forest

Nikko is a mountain town north of Tokyo, home to a spectacular complex of UNESCO World Heritage shrines and temples set among towering cedar forests. The Toshogu Shrine is famously ornate — a riot of carving and gold leaf that contrasts sharply with the usual restraint of Japanese architecture. Add waterfalls and lake scenery nearby, and Nikko is the choice for travelers who love history, temples, and forest landscapes.

Kamakura — the Great Buddha by the sea

Kamakura is a relaxed coastal town an hour or so from Tokyo, best known for its Great Buddha — a monumental bronze statue sitting in the open air. Beyond it, the town is dotted with temples and shrines, has a walkable old-town feel, and sits right by the beach. It's the easiest and most laid-back of the three, ideal if you want temples plus a sea breeze without venturing far.

Which day trip to pick

If you want mountains and Mt Fuji, choose Hakone. For grand historic shrines and forest, choose Nikko. For an easy, scenic half-to-full day with an iconic Buddha, choose Kamakura. All three are reachable by train, and a Japan Rail Pass or regional pass can make the fares more economical depending on your route.

Practical tips

Start early to make the most of the day, since travel each way eats into your time. Check the weather for Hakone especially — Mt Fuji hides behind clouds often, so a clear forecast dramatically improves the trip. Guided tours exist for all three if you'd rather not navigate the connections yourself, and they can be worth booking ahead in peak season. However you go, an early train and a little planning turn any of these into a highlight of your Tokyo stay.

title: Getting from the Airport to Central Tokyo (Narita & Haneda)
excerpt: Landing at Narita or Haneda? Here's how to get into central Tokyo, how long each takes, and which option makes sense for first-time visitors.
content:
Tokyo has two airports, and which one you land at makes a real difference to your first hour in Japan. Here's how to get from each into the center smoothly — even jet-lagged and hauling luggage.

First, know your airport

Tokyo's two gateways are Haneda (HND) and Narita (NRT). The key difference for arriving travelers: Haneda is much closer to central Tokyo, while Narita sits well outside the city. If you had a choice when booking your flight, Haneda usually means a shorter, cheaper transfer. Either way, both are well connected and easy to navigate, with clear English signage.

Set yourself up before you leave the airport

Two quick things to do on arrival before you head into the city: pick up a Suica or Pasmo IC card at a station machine (you'll use it for every train and more), and consider grabbing an eSIM or pocket WiFi so you have data immediately — both are easy to arrange at the airports. With a tap card and data, the transfer is painless.

From Haneda to central Tokyo

Haneda is the easy one — it's close, so the transfer is quick, roughly 30 minutes to central areas. Two main rail options carry you in:

  • Tokyo Monorail — connects to the JR Yamanote line at Hamamatsucho, useful for reaching stations around the loop.
  • Keikyu Line — links directly toward Shinagawa and onward, convenient for many central hotels.

Both are affordable and fast, and your IC card works on them. A taxi is an option but far pricier, worth it mainly if you're exhausted or in a group with lots of bags.

From Narita to central Tokyo

Narita is farther out, so plan on roughly 60 to 90 minutes into the center. The two standout train options:

  • Narita Express (N'EX) — a comfortable JR limited-express train running directly to major hubs like Tokyo, Shinjuku, and Shibuya stations. The simplest choice if your hotel is near one of those.
  • Keisei Skyliner — a fast train to Ueno and Nippori in the city's east, great if you're staying around Asakusa or that side of town.

There are also cheaper but slower local trains and limousine buses that go directly to many hotels — handy with heavy luggage. Avoid a straight taxi from Narita unless money is no object; the distance makes it very expensive.

Which to use

From Haneda, take the monorail or Keikyu and you'll be at your hotel fast. From Narita, match the train to your neighborhood — N'EX for the Tokyo/Shinjuku/Shibuya side, Skyliner for the Ueno/Asakusa side. Get your IC card first, and the rest is just tapping in and following the (English) signs. With the airport sorted, you're ready to dive into the city.
